title: SIU probing man's death ; Neighbours recall 'good guy' Pepper-sprayed during melee: [Ontario Edition]
article: The front porch of the east end Toronto home where Robert Walker spent his last night is cluttered with everyday trappings- a child's stroller, a bag of salt for the sidewalk.

There is also a stark reminder of the tragedy that took place on the street outside the red brick semi early Monday morning. On the glass screen door is a splotch of blood with a tiny sticker on it, identifying it as evidence.
Walker died after a violent struggle with police. His death is now under investigation.
"He was very nice, a giving person, a good guy," said Jay Rodriguez, co-owner of the home where Walker lived.

Walker, apparently emotionally distressed, ran naked into the middle of the east-end street just after midnight Monday and, according to witnesses, lunged at a circle of police officers who were trying to subdue him.

Witnesses said a blast of pepper spray did nothing to stop him. Police eventually restrained the 41-year-old and placed him in an ambulance, but he was pronounced dead shortly after arriving at St. Michael's Hospital.
Scott Gottfried, 28, a sheet metal worker who lived in the house, said he heard noises from Walker's room at around midnight and then a crashing sound on the stairs.
Rodriguez didn't want to talk about the circumstances of his friend's death. He said he was saddened and angered by the media coverage.
Rodriguez worked with Walker at an east-end snow removal company.
"I knew him as the mechanic at work," he said. "He was a good guy. I let him have a place to stay for a little while."

An inquest into Walker's death will be held, says the coroner's office, but not until the Special Investigations Unit finishes its investigation. The SIU investigates any injury, death or allegation of sexual assault that occurs during police operations.
An autopsy has been conducted on Walker, but the results are being withheld because it would "jeopardize the integrity of our investigation," said Rose Hong, a spokesperson for the SIU.
"It's pretty pertinent to what we are investigating," Hong said. "As well, we don't really have the final autopsy results because there are still toxicology tests that need to be done."

The death of Walker is similar to an incident in 2002, when Nicholas Blentzas, 24, died after being pepper-sprayed by police outside an apartment building in the Don Mills Rd. and Eglinton Ave. area. Hong said in that case SIU investigators concluded there were no reasonable grounds to believe the officers involved were criminally negligent or liable for the man's death.
A coroner's inquest into Blentzas' death has not yet been scheduled.

The use of pepper spray to subdue people who are emotionally distressed has been the subject of controversy. After three Ontario residents died in a 16-month period in the mid-1990s following police use of pepper spray, Dr. James Young, then Ontario's chief coroner, reviewed several cases. He found that most people died of heart attacks connected to a condition called excited delirium, which can be triggered by psychiatric disorders, drugs such as cocaine or acute alcohol withdrawal.
